title: Constraining the Inner Dark-Matter Slope of Sculptor: A Comparative Analysis of Dynamical Methods
comment: 30 pages, 22 figures. Code and MCMC chains: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22052154
summary: The core-cusp problem is a discrepancy between simulations and observations of the slopes of inner dark matter density profiles. The two-population estimator, separating dwarf spheroidals into metallicity-split subcomponents, is a standard method to break the mass-anisotropy degeneracy. Four dynamical methods are applied to the 1339-star Tolstoy et al. (2023) VLT/FLAMES Sculptor catalog: spherical Jeans, GravSphere, the Walker and Penarrubia (2011) two-population estimator, and a continuous $f(J,[\mathrm{Fe/H}])$ action-based distribution function. This work finds $Γ=2.49^{+0.23}_{-0.20}$, with 99.6% of the posterior lying above $Γ=2$ (84.4% after $λ$ calibration), robust to membership cuts and metal-poor contamination; GravSphere gives $γ=0.46^{+0.40}_{-0.28}$. Controlled mocks that hold tracer geometry fixed while breaking the metallicity-kinematics link attribute 77-83% of the recovered bias to geometry rather than decomposition itself; thus, mock-based claims about population splitting must control for geometry. The continuous distribution function encodes a metallicity-action coupling $k_J$ inaccessible to any split-based method; a direct action-space computation on 575 stars with Gaia proper motions finds [Fe/H] declining by 0.3 dex across three decades in radial action. On the central-density diagnostic of Read et al. (2019), the same posteriors give $ρ_{DM}(150 \mathrm{pc})=1.77 \times 10^8 M_\odot \mathrm{kpc}^{-3}$, agreeing with their independent Sculptor measurement at $0.74σ$ and placing Sculptor in their cusp-like class; the shallow $γ$ of this work is an asymptotic quantity, and the local slope at 150 pc is consistent with the Navarro-Frenk-White profile. Any tension with feedback-driven core formation therefore rests on the slope axis alone.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the core-cusp problem in dwarf spheroidal galaxies by applying four dynamical methods to the VLT/FLAMES Sculptor catalog. It finds Γ=2.49 with 99.6% of the posterior above Γ=2 (84.4% after calibration), showing that 77-83% of recovered bias in mock studies comes from tracer geometry rather than population splitting itself. Direct action-space analysis reveals a metallicity-action coupling inaccessible to split-based methods. A central density measurement ρ_DM(150pc)=1.77×10^8 M⊙/kpc⁻³ agrees with independent Sculptor measurements at 0.74σ, classifying it as cusp-like, with the shallow inner slope being an asymptotic artifact consistent with an NFW profile.
AI.motivation: The core-cusp problem represents a fundamental discrepancy between simulated and observed dark matter density profile slopes in dwarf galaxies. This work aims to resolve whether recent mock-based claims about the bias inherent to two-population estimators are genuine or artifacts of uncontrolled tracer geometry, and to provide a definitive dynamical measurement of Sculptor's inner dark matter profile using multiple independent methods.
AI.method: Four dynamical methods are applied to the 1339-star Tolstoy et al. (2023) VLT/FLAMES Sculptor catalog: (1) spherical Jeans analysis, (2) GravSphere, (3) the Walker and Penarrubia (2011) two-population estimator, and (4) a continuous f(J,[Fe/H]) action-based distribution function. Controlled mocks hold tracer geometry fixed while breaking the metallicity-kinematics link to isolate geometry effects. A direct action-space computation on 575 stars with Gaia proper motions probes metallicity-action coupling. Central density diagnostics follow the Read et al. (2019) approach.
AI.result: Γ=2.49^{+0.23}_{-0.20} with 99.6% of posterior above Γ=2 (84.4% after λ calibration), robust to membership cuts and metal-poor contamination. GravSphere yields γ=0.46^{+0.40}_{-0.28}. Mocks attribute 77-83% of recovered bias to geometry rather than decomposition. The continuous distribution function reveals a metallicity-action coupling with [Fe/H] declining 0.3 dex over three decades in radial action. The central density ρ_DM(150pc)=1.77×10^8 M⊙/kpc⁻³ agrees with Read et al. at 0.74σ, placing Sculptor in their cusp-like class.
AI.conclusion: The observed velocity dispersion profile of Sculptor is fully consistent with a cusped (NFW-like) dark matter halo. The shallow inner slope (γ) reported by some methods is an asymptotic quantity, while the local slope at 150 pc matches the NFW prediction. Mock-based claims about population splitting bias must control for tracer geometry. Any tension between observations and feedback-driven core formation rests solely on the slope axis, not on central density. This suggests Sculptor does not exhibit the core predicted by feedback simulations with standard assumptions.

title: More Numerous and Bluer: Companions of the Brightest Little Red Dots Differ from Control Galaxies at $>3σ$, Hinting at Synchronized Black Hole Seed Formation
comment: Submitted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. 10 pages, 4 figures
summary: The Little Red Dots (LRDs) are a population of compact, red sources, detected abundantly at $4 \lesssim z \lesssim 9$. While their nature is still debated, many models suggest they are powered by accreting massive black holes. Multiple studies have detected blue companions in their vicinity, motivating our analysis: we compare $253$ LRDs uniformly selected across several JWST deep fields against $>7000$ matched controls in the same mosaics. We find that $27.7\%$ of the brightest LRD quartile host a blue ($β<-1$) companion at $0.5-2$ kpc, versus $11.6\%$ of redshift-matched controls: a $\times 2.39$ excess, significant at $3.3σ$. This phenomenon is limited to the brightest LRDs, as the full LRD sample pairs at a rate indistinguishable from controls. Moreover, the excess is confined to the close-pair window ($< 2$ kpc), outside which LRD environments are ordinary. The companions of the brightest LRDs are overwhelmingly ($92\%$) blue, and significantly bluer, with a median $β\approx-2.32$, versus $β\approx-1.92$ for those of controls, rejecting a common parent distribution at $3.4σ$. The signal is thus directional in three independent ways: luminosity, separation, and companion color, all expected for synchronized-pair seed formation. Therefore, we conclude that the association between the brightest LRDs and their close blue companions is physical, i.e., the two phenomena are causally connected: either one drives the other, or both emerge from the same synchronized formation event. A natural explanation for why the most luminous LRDs have nearby, young, star-forming neighbors is that the radiation from these neighbors enabled the direct collapse of the massive black holes powering the LRDs themselves.

AI.tldr: The authors compare 253 Little Red Dots (LRDs) against >7000 matched controls in JWST deep fields, finding that the brightest LRD quartile show a 2.39x excess of close blue companions within 0.5-2 kpc, significant at 3.3σ. The excess is directional in luminosity, separation, and companion color, suggesting the association is physical and causal—possibly that radiation from these young star-forming neighbors enabled direct collapse of the massive black holes powering the LRDs.
AI.motivation: LRDs are abundant compact red sources at 4≲z≲9, with many models suggesting accreting massive black holes as their power source. Previous studies detected blue companions near them, motivating a systematic, statistically rigorous investigation of whether this association is physical or coincidental.
AI.method: Uniform selection of 253 LRDs across multiple JWST deep fields, compared against >7000 redshift-matched controls in the same mosaics. The analysis tests excess companion presence as a function of LRD brightness, projected separation, and companion color (β index).
AI.result: Brightest LRD quartile host blue companions at 0.5-2 kpc at 27.7% vs 11.6% for controls (2.39x excess, 3.3σ). The excess disappears for fainter LRDs and beyond 2 kpc. Companion colors differ significantly (median β≈-2.32 vs -1.92, rejected at 3.4σ), with 92% of LRD companions being blue.
AI.conclusion: The association between brightest LRDs and close blue companions is physical and causally connected. Most plausible explanation is synchronized-pair seed formation where radiation from young star-forming neighbors enabled direct collapse of massive black holes powering the LRDs.

title: Spin inference with the Black Hole Explorer. I. Fisher information matrix forecast
summary: General relativity predicts the presence of a thin, bright ring of light superimposed on the image of a black hole (the ``photon ring''), whose geometry is sensitive to the spin of the black hole. Detecting this photon ring in observations of nuclear supermassive black holes would yield insight into gravity in the strong-field regime as well as their growth histories. The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) is a mission being developed to detect the photon ring for the first time, raising the question of how precisely we can constrain spin from its observations. We use the method of Fisher information matrices (FIMs) along with a simple dual-cone semi-analytic emission model to forecast BHEX spin posterior widths for the primary science targets (M87* and Sgr~A*) in a variety of configurations. We find that BHEX can constrain the dimensionless spin of its targets to a precision of $σ_{a_*} \ll 0.1$ after 30 orbits, even in the presence of significant systematic errors. We validate our results via numerical checks for stability and robustness, as well as synthetic data cross-validation to assess handling of covariances and prior information in the FIM against a full posterior exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper forecasts that the Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) mission can constrain the dimensionless spin of supermassive black holes M87* and Sgr A* to a precision far better than 0.1 after 30 orbits, using Fisher information matrices with a dual-cone emission model, even in the presence of significant systematic errors.
AI.motivation: Detecting the photon ring predicted by general relativity in black hole images would provide insight into strong-field gravity and black hole growth histories. The BHEX mission aims to detect the photon ring for the first time, raising the question of how precisely spin can be constrained from its observations.
AI.method: The study uses Fisher information matrices (FIMs) combined with a simple dual-cone semi-analytic emission model to forecast BHEX spin posterior widths for the primary science targets (M87* and Sgr A*) across various observation configurations. Validation includes numerical stability and robustness checks, plus synthetic data cross-validation comparing FIM covariance and prior handling against a full posterior exploration.
AI.result: BHEX can constrain the dimensionless spin of its targets to a precision of σ_{a*} ≪ 0.1 after 30 orbits, even in the presence of significant systematic errors. The forecasts are validated through numerical stability/robustness checks and synthetic data cross-validation.
AI.conclusion: The BHEX mission is capable of delivering extremely precise spin measurements for M87* and Sgr A*, enabling detection of the photon ring and providing strong constraints on strong-field gravity and black hole growth histories.

title: A simulation-based quality-control framework for the broad-line region radius-luminosity relation
summary: The broad-line region (BLR) radius-luminosity (R-L) relation underpins single-epoch black hole mass estimates in active galactic nuclei (AGN). The published Hβsample is heterogeneous in observational quality, and it remains unclear how much of its scatter is intrinsic rather than caused by systematics in lag recovery. We quantify the contribution of unreliable lag recovery to the observed scatter of the HβR-L relation and provide tools for quality control. We compile a publicly available database of reverberation mapping measurements for ~1200 AGN from 32 campaigns spanning more than three decades, including lags, luminosities, line widths, black hole masses, and observational metadata. We develop a simulation-based consistency framework in which damped random walk light curves are sampled according to each campaign's baseline, cadence, and signal-to-noise ratio, and lags are recovered with the interpolated cross-correlation function (ICCF). Comparing expected, reported, and simulation-retrieved lags defines a four-tier flagging scheme. We refit the R-L relation with UltraNest for progressively cleaner samples and construct consensus samples across three reference slopes to reduce model dependence. Of 248 Hβsources, ~40% show discrepancies between reported and simulation-retrieved lags, while ~5% show direct inconsistencies between expected and retrieved lags. Excluding flagged sources and correcting for model bias reduces the inferred intrinsic scatter from σ= 0.26^{+0.02}_{-0.01} dex to 0.11\pm0.01 dex, with a corrected slope of α= 0.48\pm0.02. Our results indicate that a substantial fraction of the observed HβR-L scatter arises from observational limitations and lag-recovery biases rather than intrinsic AGN diversity. The database, simulation code, and RM-Scout campaign-planning tool are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how much of the scatter in the Hβ broad-line region radius-luminosity (R-L) relation is due to unreliable lag recovery rather than intrinsic AGN diversity. Using a database of ~1200 reverberation-mapping AGN from 32 campaigns, the authors build a simulation-based quality-control framework, flag unreliable lag measurements, and show that intrinsic scatter drops from 0.26 to 0.11 dex with a corrected slope of α=0.48±0.02.
AI.motivation: The Hβ R-L relation is critical for single-epoch black hole mass estimates, but the published sample is heterogeneous in observational quality. It is unclear whether the observed scatter in this relation is intrinsic to AGN or an artifact of systematics in lag recovery, so a systematic quantification is needed.
AI.method: The authors compile a public database of ~1200 AGN from 32 reverberation-mapping campaigns (lags, luminosities, line widths, masses, and metadata). They build a simulation-based consistency framework: damped random walk light curves are sampled per each campaign's baseline, cadence, and S/N, and lags are recovered via the interpolated cross-correlation function (ICCF). Comparing expected, reported, and simulation-retrieved lags yields a four-tier flagging scheme. The R-L relation is refit with UltraNest on progressively cleaner samples, with consensus samples constructed across three reference slopes.
AI.result: Of 248 Hβ sources, ~40% show discrepancies between reported and simulation-retrieved lags, and ~5% show direct inconsistencies between expected and retrieved lags. After flagging and bias correction, the intrinsic scatter decreases from σ=0.26+0.02/−0.01 to 0.11±0.01 dex, with a corrected slope α=0.48±0.02.
AI.conclusion: A substantial fraction of the observed Hβ R-L scatter is attributable to observational limitations and lag-recovery biases rather than intrinsic AGN diversity. The database, simulation code, and RM-Scout planning tool are made publicly available for quality control in future reverberation-mapping studies.

title: CosmoFit: A Graphical User Interface for Bayesian Cosmological Parameter Estimation with User-Defined H(z) Models
summary: We present CosmoFit, a desktop graphical interface for Bayesian parameter inference in background cosmology. The application is designed to simplify cosmological analyses by reducing the need to manually program each step, while maintaining the transparency and reproducibility of the results. Users can define an expansion history H(z), specify fixed and sampled parameters, assign prior ranges and proposal scales, select the available observational likelihoods, and run Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses from a unified graphical interface. CosmoFit uses Cobaya for Bayesian sampling and GetDist for posterior analysis and visualization. The current version supports cosmic-chronometer data and the official Pantheon+, Pantheon+SH0ES, and Union3 supernova likelihoods available through Cobaya. For each run, the application stores the configuration files, metadata, execution logs, chains, and numerical summaries required to inspect and reproduce the analysis. The performance of CosmoFit was evaluated through unit tests, a parameter-recovery test using synthetic data, and an independent comparison with an analysis performed directly in Cobaya. The posterior mean values obtained with both procedures agree to within less than one percent. In addition, the synthetic-data test recovers the fiducial parameters within the expected credible regions. As an illustrative example, we perform a spatially flat wCDM analysis using Pantheon+SH0ES and obtain marginalized constraints and triangle plots directly from the interface. Within its current scope, CosmoFit provides an accessible, transparent, and reproducible tool for research and academic applications involving explicit models of the background cosmological expansion.

AI.tldr: CosmoFit is a desktop GUI for Bayesian parameter inference in background cosmology, providing a unified graphical interface for defining expansion histories, setting priors and parameters, selecting observational likelihoods, and running MCMC analyses via Cobaya sampling and GetDist visualization. Validity confirmed through unit tests, synthetic-data recovery, and agreement within 1% against direct Cobaya analysis.
AI.motivation: To simplify cosmological Bayesian analyses by reducing the need for manual programming at each step, while maintaining transparency and reproducibility of results for research and academic applications.
AI.method: A desktop graphical interface where users can define H(z), specify fixed/sampled parameters, assign priors and proposal scales, select observational likelihoods (cosmic chronometers, Pantheon+, Pantheon+SH0ES, Union3), and run MCMC chains. Built on Cobaya for sampling and GetDist for posterior analysis and visualization, with automatic storage of configuration files, metadata, logs, chains, and summaries.
AI.result: Unit tests passed; synthetic-data test recovered fiducial parameters within credible regions; independent comparison with direct Cobaya analysis showed posterior means agreeing within less than one percent. An illustrative flat wCDM analysis with Pantheon+SH0ES produced marginalized constraints and triangle plots directly from the interface.
AI.conclusion: CosmoFit provides an accessible, transparent, and reproducible tool for research and academic applications involving explicit models of the background cosmological expansion within its current scope.

title: Cool CGM MgII Absorption Across the Star-Forming, Green Valley, and Quiescent Transition
summary: We investigate the distribution and kinematics of cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) gas across the star-forming to quiescent transition using MgII absorption for 716 galaxies spanning $0.07<z<2.7$ (169 new and 547 archival galaxies). To compare galaxies uniformly across 10 billion years of cosmic time, we introduce a star-formation offset metric ($σ_{\mathrm{SFO}}$), which measures a galaxy's deviation from the star-forming main sequence of its epoch. A key advantage of $σ_{\mathrm{SFO}}$ is its ability to identify transitional green valley galaxies as a distinct population across redshift, which would otherwise be obscured by binary star-forming-passive classifications. We fit a virial-radius-normalized radial profile and find that the MgII absorption strength declines with increasing projected distance from the host galaxy. The scatter around this mean profile correlates strongly with star-formation activity: radial profile residuals correlate positively with $\log sSFR$ and $σ_{\mathrm{SFO}}$, with star-forming galaxies showing excess absorption above the profile, green-valley galaxies showing intermediate residuals, and quiescent galaxies falling preferentially below it. The MgII covering fraction in the inner CGM ($R/R_{200} < 0.25$) follows the same sequence, declining monotonically from star-forming through green-valley to quiescent systems. MgII absorption kinematics are consistent with a predominantly bound cool CGM. Star-forming galaxies further exhibit a bimodal azimuthal dependence, with MgII absorption enhanced along both the polar and disk directions, consistent with bipolar outflows and co-planar accretion. Together, these results indicate that the cool CGM tracks the quenching of star-formation in galaxies, with $σ_{\mathrm{SFO}}$ revealing a gradual decline in cool gas across the green valley rather than an abrupt star-forming-to-passive transition.

AI.tldr: This study examines the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) across the star-forming to quiescent transition using MgII absorption for 716 galaxies over 0.07<z<2.7. The authors introduce a star-formation offset metric (σ_SFO) that identifies green valley galaxies as a distinct population across redshift. They find that MgII absorption declines with projected radius, correlates with star-formation activity, and reveals a gradual decline in cool CGM gas across the green valley rather than an abrupt transition.
AI.motivation: To understand how the cool CGM evolves as galaxies transition from star-forming to quiescent, using a metric that can uniformly compare galaxies across ~10 billion years of cosmic time and identify transitional green valley galaxies that binary classifications would obscure.
AI.method: Analysis of MgII absorption for 716 galaxies (169 new, 547 archival) spanning 0.07<z<2.7, using a newly introduced star-formation offset metric (σ_SFO) measuring deviation from the epoch-dependent star-forming main sequence. Radial profiles are virial-radius-normalized, with residuals and covering fractions computed within the inner CGM, alongside kinematic and azimuthal dependence analysis.
AI.result: MgII absorption declines with projected radius; radial profile residuals correlate with log sSFR and σ_SFO, with star-forming galaxies showing excess absorption, green-valley galaxies intermediate residuals, and quiescent galaxies below the profile. Covering fraction declines monotonically from star-forming through green-valley to quiescent systems. Kinematics show a predominantly bound cool CGM, and star-forming galaxies exhibit bimodal azimuthal absorption consistent with bipolar outflows and co-planar accretion.
AI.conclusion: The cool CGM tracks galaxy quenching, and σ_SFO reveals the decline in cool gas across the green valley is gradual rather than abrupt, indicating a smooth transition in CGM properties throughout the quenching process.

title: Exact Equivalence of the Observed Redshift and the Pulsar Timing Modulation in the Infinitesimal-Pulse Limit
summary: The pulsar timing arrays (PTA) collect the times of arrival of radio signals from the millisecond pulsars, and gravitational waves can modulate their arrival times. Although the PTA observable involves successive radio pulses propagating along different light paths, its standard theoretical description at linear order in perturbations is equivalent to the Sachs-Wolfe formula for the observed redshift, which describes the fractional change in photon frequency along a single geodesic. While this equivalence is well known at linear order, its validity beyond first order has not been systematically addressed in the PTA literature. Here we show that, in the limit of vanishing proper-time separation between successive emission events, the timing modulation is exactly equal to the observed redshift, without expanding the spacetime geometry. For a finite emission interval, we derive the exact relation between the timing modulation and the observed redshift, and show that their difference is controlled by the ratio between the emission interval and the characteristic timescale over which the observed redshift varies.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously establishes the relationship between pulsar timing array (PTA) timing modulations and the observed gravitational-wave redshift, showing that in the limit of vanishing proper-time separation between successive emission events the timing modulation equals the observed redshift exactly (beyond linear order), and deriving an exact relation for finite emission intervals where the difference is controlled by the ratio of the emission interval to the characteristic timescale of redshift variation.
AI.motivation: While the equivalence between PTA timing modulation and the Sachs-Wolfe redshift formula is well established at linear order in perturbations, its validity beyond first order has not been systematically addressed in the PTA literature. This work fills that gap by examining the exact (non-perturbative) relationship between the PTA observable and the observed redshift.
AI.method: The authors analyze the PTA timing modulation without expanding the spacetime geometry. They consider two regimes: (1) the limit of vanishing proper-time separation between successive emission events, where they prove the timing modulation equals the observed redshift exactly; and (2) finite emission intervals, where they derive an exact relation between timing modulation and observed redshift, showing the difference is governed by the ratio between the emission interval and the characteristic timescale of redshift variation.
AI.result: The authors prove that in the zero-emission-interval limit, the PTA timing modulation is exactly equal to the observed redshift at all orders (beyond linear perturbation theory). For finite emission intervals, they derive an exact formula connecting the two quantities, with corrections controlled by the ratio of emission interval to the characteristic redshift-variation timescale.
AI.conclusion: The equivalence between PTA timing modulation and gravitational-wave-induced redshift extends beyond linear order in the vanishing emission-interval limit, providing a rigorous non-perturbative foundation for the standard PTA response description. For realistic finite emission intervals, the deviation from this equivalence is systematically characterized and suppressed by the timescale ratio.

title: The Evolution of Low-Ionization Electron Densities in Galaxies Across Cosmic Epochs
summary: We investigate the low-ionization electron density in the interstellar medium of galaxies across $0$$<$$z$$<$$8$, derived with the [O II]$λ\lambda3727,3730$ and [S II]$λ\lambda6718,6733$ doublets, using both deep JWST NIRCam/grism and NIRSpec/MSA spectroscopy. Along with ancillary density samples from the literature at $0$$<$$z$$<$$6$, we assemble three samples containing a total of 703 galaxies spanning $3.7$$<$$z$$<$$7.8$ at $\langle z\rangle\sim5.6$; 691 galaxies in the luminosity-complete NIRCam/grism programs CONGRESS and FRESCO at $\langle z\rangle \sim4.3$ and $\langle z\rangle\sim5.3$, respectively, and 12 galaxies with high-resolution NIRSpec/MSA spectra from the GO 1871 and GLASS programs. We find median electron densities of $n_{\rm{e}}$[S II]$=$$463^{+281}_{-203}~{\rm{cm}}^{-3}$ for CONGRESS, $n_{\rm{e}}$[S II]$=$$301^{+388}_{-206}~{\rm{cm}}^{-3}$ for FRESCO, and $n_{\rm{e}}$[O II]$=$$202^{+145}_{-102}~{\rm{cm}}^{-3}$ for the NIRSpec/MSA sample. The median low-ionization $n_{\rm{e}}$ increases from $z= 0$ to $z=4$, in agreement with previous studies and those using JWST observations. However, beyond $z\sim4$ median $n_{\rm{e}}$ begins to deviate from a monotonically increasing evolution with $z$. We find a positive, but shallow, correlation between O$_{32}$ (a proxy for the ionization parameter) and $n_{\rm{e}}$, while also confirming a positive correlation between O$_{32}$ and $z$. We suggest that these trends are possibly due to an evolving ISM gas density and ionization structure, and propose a toy model where the gas clumping evolves with $z$ to explain the observed density and ionization variations.

AI.tldr: This paper measures low-ionization electron densities in the ISM of 703 galaxies at 3.7<z<7.8 using JWST NIRCam/grism and NIRSpec/MSA spectroscopy with [O II] and [S II] doublets, finding median densities of 463 cm^-3 (CONGRESS), 301 cm^-3 (FRESCO), and 202 cm^-3 (NIRSpec/MSA). The density increases from z=0 to z~4 but deviates from monotonic growth beyond z~4. A shallow positive O32-ne correlation is found, and a toy model with evolving gas clumping is proposed to explain observed trends.
AI.motivation: To characterize the evolution of electron density (and hence ISM physical conditions) in low-ionization gas across cosmic time, extending density measurements to the epoch of reionization (z~4-8) using deep JWST observations, and to investigate how the ISM density and ionization structure evolve with redshift.
AI.method: The analysis combines three samples: (1) 691 galaxies from luminosity-complete NIRCam/grism programs CONGRESS (z~4.3) and FRESCO (z~5.3), spanning 3.7<z<7.8; (2) 12 galaxies with high-resolution NIRSpec/MSA spectra from GO 1871 and GLASS; and (3) ancillary literature samples at 0<z<6. Electron densities are derived using [O II]λλ3727,3730 and [S II]λλ6718,6733 doublet ratios. Correlations between O32 (ionization parameter proxy) and n_e, and between O32 and z, are examined, supplemented by a toy model of evolving gas clumping.
AI.result: Median electron densities of n_e[S II]=463^{+281}_{-203} cm^-3 (CONGRESS), n_e[S II]=301^{+388}_{-206} cm^-3 (FRESCO), and n_e[O II]=202^{+145}_{-102} cm^-3 (NIRSpec/MSA). Median low-ionization n_e increases from z=0 to z~4 in agreement with prior studies, but deviates from monotonic evolution beyond z~4. A positive but shallow O32-n_e correlation is found, along with a confirmed positive O32-z correlation.
AI.conclusion: The evolving electron density and ionization parameter trends suggest changes in ISM gas density and ionization structure with redshift, possibly driven by the redshift evolution of gas clumping. The authors propose a toy model where gas clumping evolves with z to explain the observed density and ionization variations.

title: Beyond $w_0-w_a$ and Phantom Crossing: Testing Models of Coupled Dark Sector
summary: The combination of cosmic microwave background (CMB) measurements with distance measurements from baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and type Ia supernovae (SNIa) suggests that dark energy is dynamical, with an equation of state crossing the phantom divide at low redshifts. This feature can not be described within canonically normalized, minimally coupled, self-interacting scalar field models. We investigate the possibility of achieving phantom crossing by introducing an interaction in the dark sector such that the dark matter particle mass is dependent on the dark energy field $φ$ as $m \propto φ^α$. We consider a self-interacting potential of the inverse power-law form $V \propto φ^{-β}$. We implement this model both at the background and perturbative levels in a Boltzmann solver and use a bayesian framework to constrain its parameters using using CMB, BAO and SNIa data. We find best-fits that have similar goodness-of-fits as the commonly used phenomenological $w_0-w_a$ parameterization, providing a more fundamental understanding of the dark sector.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a dynamical dark energy model where phantom crossing can occur via an interaction between dark matter and dark energy, with dark matter particle mass dependent on the scalar field (m ∝ φ^α) and an inverse power-law potential (V ∝ φ^-β). The model is constrained using CMB, BAO, and SNIa data in a Bayesian framework, achieving fits comparable to the phenomenological w0-wa parameterization.
AI.motivation: CMB data combined with BAO and SNIa distances suggest dark energy is dynamical with an equation of state crossing the phantom divide at low redshifts, a feature that cannot be described by canonical scalar field models. The authors aim to provide a more fundamental physical explanation for this observed behavior.
AI.method: The model introduces an interaction where dark matter particle mass depends on the dark energy scalar field as m ∝ φ^α, with a self-interacting potential of the form V ∝ φ^-β. The model is implemented at both background and perturbative levels in a Boltzmann solver and constrained using a Bayesian framework with CMB, BAO, and SNIa data.
AI.result: The best-fit parameters from this interacting dark sector model achieve goodness-of-fit values comparable to the standard phenomenological w0-wa parameterization, while providing a more fundamental physical understanding of the dark sector.
AI.conclusion: The interacting dark energy-dark matter model successfully describes the observed phantom crossing without requiring exotic physics, and offers a viable alternative to purely phenomenological parameterizations with equivalent statistical performance.

title: The Local Origin of a Host Dispersion Measure-Stellar Mass Relation in Fast Radio Bursts
summary: The origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) and the relationship to their host galaxy environments remain open questions. Using a sample of 37 FRBs with secure host associations at $z \lesssim 0.25$, and including dwarf, elliptical, and edge-on hosts, we examine the host dispersion measure ($\mathrm{DM_{host}}$) and its dependence on host stellar mass ($M_\star$). We find a statistically significant anti-correlation between the host dispersion measure and host stellar mass (the $\mathrm{DM_{host}}$-$M_\star$ relation; Pearson $r \approx -0.5$, $\log_{10} p \approx -2.8$) that extends across the full range of our sample, $\log_{10}(M_\star/M_\odot) \approx 8$-$11.4$. We find that the rest-frame Faraday rotation measure ($|\mathrm{RM}|_{\mathrm{host}}$) is largest in FRBs that reside in dwarf galaxies, but there is no evidence for a correlation across the full mass range. We show that the $\mathrm{DM_{host}}$-$M_\star$ trend does not arise from the galaxy-averaged interstellar medium (ISM) nor from the circumgalactic medium (CGM). Instead, we argue that the local ($\lesssim 100$ pc) environment is responsible. The spatial statistics of star formation and metallicity-dependent FRB progenitor channels plausibly lead to denser ionized environments in low-mass galaxies and less nearby gas in massive hosts.

AI.tldr: Analyzing 37 FRBs with secure host associations at z≲0.25, the paper finds a statistically significant anti-correlation between host dispersion measure (DM_host) and host stellar mass (M⋆), and argues this trend originates from the local (<100 pc) environment rather than galaxy-averaged ISM or CGM, likely due to star formation spatial statistics and metallicity-dependent FRB progenitor channels.
AI.motivation: The origin of fast radio bursts (FRBs) and their relationship to host galaxy environments remain open questions. This paper aims to understand how host galaxy properties, particularly stellar mass, influence the dispersion measure of FRBs and to determine which component of the host environment (local, ISM, or CGM) drives the observed relationship.
AI.method: Using a sample of 37 FRBs with secure host galaxy associations at z≲0.25, spanning dwarf, elliptical, and edge-on hosts, the authors examine the host dispersion measure (DM_host) as a function of host stellar mass (M⋆) across the range log10(M⋆/M⊙)≈8–11.4. They compute Pearson correlation coefficients and also examine rest-frame Faraday rotation measures (|RM|_host) across the sample.
AI.result: A statistically significant anti-correlation is found between DM_host and M⋆ (Pearson r≈-0.5, log10 p≈-2.8) spanning the full mass range. The rest-frame |RM|_host is largest in FRBs residing in dwarf galaxies, but no correlation is found across the full mass range. The DM_host-M⋆ trend is shown not to arise from galaxy-averaged ISM or CGM contributions.
AI.conclusion: The DM_host-M⋆ anti-correlation is driven by the local (<100 pc) environment around each FRB. The spatial statistics of star formation and metallicity-dependent FRB progenitor channels plausibly produce denser ionized environments in low-mass galaxies and less nearby gas in massive hosts, explaining the observed trend.

title: A New Probe of Dark Matter Subhalos: Stellar Aberration with TESS
summary: Small-scale dark matter (DM) structure encodes key information about the particle nature of DM and therefore provides a sensitive test of competing models. Yet, it remains hidden from electromagnetic surveys and is instead inferred through its gravitational effects. Stellar aberration, the apparent shift in a light source's position induced by the observer's motion, offers a largely unexplored channel to access such signatures. DM subhalos can perturb the observer's motion, imprinting characteristic, spatially correlated shifts in stellar positions across the sky. We show that the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), with its long temporal baseline, wide sky coverage, and high-cadence observations, is well suited to search for these aberration signals. We derive Fisher-matrix-based sensitivity estimates for constant observer accelerations, forecasting a sensitivity down to $6.3\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ from the combined sample of TESS stars with magnitude $\mathrm{Tmag}\leq 10$. This sensitivity allows TESS to probe concentrated DM subhalos over a broad parameter space, from $\gtrsim 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$ at AU-scale distances to $\gtrsim 10^{7}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$ at $\mathcal{O}(10\,\mathrm{pc})$. TESS's sector-based observing strategy further provides intrinsic temporal resolution of potential DM-induced aberration signals. Moreover, we briefly discuss challenges for future data analysis, including the modeling of instrumental systematics and stellar astrometric foregrounds, such as parallax and proper motion. Our results establish stellar aberration as a novel probe of DM substructure, paving the way for dedicated searches in TESS and next-generation wide-field surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using stellar aberration—apparent shifts in stellar positions due to observer motion induced by dark matter subhalos—as a novel probe of small-scale DM structure. Using the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), the authors forecast sensitivity to constant observer accelerations down to 6.3×10⁻⁹ m/s², enabling detection of DM subhalos from ~10⁻⁶ M☉ at AU scales to ~10⁷ M☉ at ~10 pc distances.
AI.motivation: Small-scale DM structure encodes crucial information about the particle nature of dark matter, but remains hidden from electromagnetic surveys and can only be probed via gravitational effects. Stellar aberration induced by DM subhalos perturbing the observer's motion offers a largely unexplored channel to access these signatures, and TESS's long baseline, wide coverage, and high cadence make it well suited to this search.
AI.method: The authors derive Fisher-matrix-based sensitivity estimates for constant observer accelerations using TESS observations of stars with Tmag ≤ 10. They analyze TESS's sector-based observing strategy for temporal resolution of potential DM-induced aberration signals and discuss modeling challenges including instrumental systematics, stellar parallax, and proper motion foregrounds.
AI.result: The analysis forecasts a sensitivity down to 6.3×10⁻⁹ m/s² from the combined TESS stellar sample, allowing TESS to probe concentrated DM subhalos across a broad parameter space: from ≳10⁻⁶ M☉ at AU-scale distances to ≳10⁷ M☉ at O(10 pc) scales.
AI.conclusion: Stellar aberration is established as a novel probe of DM substructure, with TESS providing a viable observational platform now and paving the way for dedicated searches in TESS and next-generation wide-field surveys.

title: Comparing the Nebular and Stellar Dust Attenuation Curves in Nearby Star-Forming Galaxies
comment: Accepted by Journal of the Korean Astronomical Society, 12 pages, 7 figures
summary: Differences in the spatial distributions of stars and ionized gas relative to dust in galaxies imply that stellar and nebular dust attenuation curves need not be identical. Although stellar attenuation curves have been extensively studied, nebular attenuation curves remain less explored. In this work, we investigate nebular attenuation curves using Balmer line ratios for a sample of 90,958 nearby star-forming galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey with well-constrained stellar attenuation curves. In the H$α$/H$β$ versus H$α$/H$γ$ diagram, the nebular attenuation curves are, on average, significantly shallower than typical stellar attenuation curves, which can be qualitatively reproduced by source-dust geometric effects. The nebular attenuation curve slopes show weak positive correlations with the stellar attenuation curve slopes and weak dependences on galaxy properties that broadly follow those of the stellar attenuation curve slopes. These results suggest that nebular attenuation curves are distinct from stellar attenuation curves, while remaining consistent with a connection between them.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes nebular dust attenuation curves using Balmer line ratios from 90,958 nearby star-forming galaxies in SDSS, finding that nebular attenuation curves are significantly shallower than stellar attenuation curves, with weak positive correlations to stellar curve slopes and galaxy properties, suggesting they are distinct but connected.
AI.motivation: While stellar dust attenuation curves have been extensively studied, nebular attenuation curves remain less explored. Understanding the differences between stellar and nebular attenuation is important because spatial distributions of stars and ionized gas relative to dust differ in galaxies, implying the two attenuation curves need not be identical.
AI.method: Using Balmer line ratios (Hα/Hβ and Hα/Hγ) for a sample of 90,958 nearby star-forming galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, the authors investigate nebular attenuation curves and compare them with well-constrained stellar attenuation curves for the same galaxies.
AI.result: The nebular attenuation curves are on average significantly shallower than typical stellar attenuation curves, a difference qualitatively reproduced by source-dust geometric effects. Nebular curve slopes show weak positive correlations with stellar curve slopes and weak dependences on galaxy properties broadly following stellar attenuation curve slopes.
AI.conclusion: Nebular attenuation curves are distinct from stellar attenuation curves, yet remain consistent with a connection between them, implying that different dust attenuation prescriptions are needed for stellar and nebular emission.

title: Projected Constraints on Primordial Black Holes from Scalar-Induced Gravitational Waves with Taiji
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Submit to Sci.China Phys.Mech.Astron
summary: Scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) provide a direct probe of the enhanced primordial curvature perturbations that may also produce primordial black holes (PBHs). We forecast the capability of the space-based gravitational-wave observatory Taiji to search for an SIGW background generated by a broken-power-law curvature spectrum. A signal-injection study is used to validate the analysis pipeline, after which a pure-noise realization is employed to derive projected upper limits on the curvature-spectrum parameters. We translate these limits into constraints on the PBH abundance using the nonlinear compaction function, critical collapse, and the joint Gaussian distribution of the compaction amplitude and curvature at its peak. The resulting projected $95\%$ upper limits on the PBH dark-matter fraction satisfy $f_{\mathrm{PBH}}^{95\%}<1$ over PBH masses from approximately $6.2\times10^{-18}\,M_\odot$ to $1.7\times10^{-8}\,M_\odot$. We compare the forecast with representative Hawking-evaporation and microlensing bounds. In part of the asteroid-mass interval, the projected Taiji limit is more restrictive than the current Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) microlensing constraint.

AI.tldr: The paper forecasts the capability of the space-based gravitational-wave observatory Taiji to detect scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) from a broken-power-law curvature power spectrum. Using signal-injection validation and pure-noise realizations, it derives projected 95% upper limits on PBH dark-matter fraction across ~6.2×10^-18 to 1.7×10^-8 solar masses, finding that Taiji could outperform current HSC microlensing constraints in part of the asteroid-mass range.
AI.motivation: SIGWs offer a direct observational probe of enhanced primordial curvature perturbations, which may also produce primordial black holes. Constraining PBH abundance through gravitational-wave signatures complements existing indirect detection methods such as Hawking evaporation and microlensing.
AI.method: The authors use a signal-injection study to validate their analysis pipeline, then apply the pipeline to a pure-noise realization to derive projected upper limits on the broken-power-law curvature-spectrum parameters. These are translated into PBH abundance constraints using the nonlinear compaction function formalism, critical collapse, and the joint Gaussian distribution of compaction amplitude and curvature at its peak.
AI.result: The projected 95% upper limits on the PBH dark-matter fraction satisfy f_PBH<1 over PBH masses from ~6.2×10^-18 to 1.7×10^-8 solar masses. In part of the asteroid-mass interval, the projected Taiji sensitivity is more restrictive than the current Subaru HSC microlensing constraint.
AI.conclusion: Taiji has strong potential to probe SIGW backgrounds from broken-power-law curvature spectra and to competitively constrain PBH abundances in the asteroid-mass range, complementing and in some regimes exceeding existing observational bounds.

title: Interplay of Compaction, Quenching, and Black Hole Growth in the Most Massive Galaxies since $z\sim5$: Insights from JWST and Chandra Data
summary: The buildup of dense stellar cores is expected to mark an important transition in the star-formation and black-hole growth of massive galaxies. Using spatially resolved spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting of James Webb Space Telescope near-infrared imaging, combined with stacking analysis of Chandra X-ray data, we trace stellar mass buildup and average black hole accretion in the most massive galaxies at $z<5$, selecting 50 most massive galaxies per redshift bin at constant number density of $\sim4.4\times10^{-5}$ cMpc$^{-3}$. To robustly constrain central stellar populations, we separate active galactic nuclei (AGN) components affecting the photometry using multi-band morphological decomposition and SED analysis. We find that the sample selected with constant number density exhibits evolutionary trend of rapid central compaction at $z\sim4$, during which the median central 1 kpc stellar mass increases by $\sim0.60$ dex over $\sim400$ Myr. The majority of X-ray detected AGN ($63\%\pm12\%$) are hosted by galaxies undergoing the compaction, while we find neither individually detected X-ray sources nor a significant stacked X-ray signal at $z>4$, indicating that substantial average black-hole growth emerges primarily during, rather than before, the compaction. Following the compaction, central specific star formation rates (sSFR) decline by $\sim1.24$ dex over $\sim700$ Myr at $z\sim3$ while remaining elevated galaxy-wide, signaling the onset of inside-out quenching. Despite this central suppression, specific black hole accretion rate remains coupled to the total sSFR. Our results suggest that dense-core formation in the most massive galaxies marks the onset of inside-out quenching and a transition toward enhanced black-hole to stellar growth ratio.

AI.tldr: Using JWST NIR imaging and Chandra X-ray stacking, this study follows the 50 most massive galaxies per redshift bin at z<5 (constant number density ~4.4e-5 cMpc^-3) and finds that dense-core formation at z~4 (central 1 kpc stellar mass increases ~0.60 dex over ~400 Myr) marks the onset of inside-out quenching and a transition toward enhanced black-hole growth relative to star formation.
AI.motivation: To understand when and how massive galaxies build their dense stellar cores, and whether this process triggers inside-out quenching and transitions black-hole growth relative to star formation.
AI.method: Spatially resolved SED fitting of JWST near-infrared imaging combined with Chandra X-ray stacking analysis, selecting the 50 most massive galaxies per redshift bin at constant number density (z<5). Multi-band morphological decomposition and SED analysis are used to separate AGN contamination from central stellar populations.
AI.result: The sample shows rapid central compaction at z~4 (central stellar mass +0.60 dex over ~400 Myr). Most X-ray AGN (63%±12%) are hosted by compacting galaxies, but no X-ray sources or stacked signal are found at z>4. After compaction, central sSFR declines ~1.24 dex over ~700 Myr at z~3 with galaxy-wide sSFR remaining elevated (inside-out quenching), while specific black hole accretion remains coupled to total sSFR.
AI.conclusion: Dense-core formation in the most massive galaxies marks the onset of inside-out quenching and a transition toward an enhanced black-hole-to-stellar growth ratio; substantial black hole growth emerges primarily during, not before, the compaction phase.

title: The Effect of Slitless Spectroscopic Redshift Uncertainty and Interlopers on BAO Measurements from CSST-like Samples
comment: 14 pages, 6 (and 7 supplementary) figures, accepted by MNRAS
summary: The baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) is a vital probe to measure cosmological distances and constrain dark energy. The ongoing and near-future space-based telescopes, including the Chinese Space Station Survey Telescope (CSST), will perform galaxy redshift surveys using slitless spectroscopy. Due to the relatively low spectral resolution and observational effects, there will be uncertainties and interloper contamination in measured redshifts. In this study, we consider the Gaussian-distributed redshift uncertainty and [O III]-H$β$ interlopers in the CSST-like slitless spectroscopic redshift (spec-z) samples, which are simulated using the approximate $N$-body code FastPM. We study the effect of spec-z errors on BAO before and after density field reconstruction. Both the redshift uncertainty and interlopers can damp the BAO signal, and the latter can further induce oscillations in the broadband shape of the power spectrum. We model the interloper effect on the propagator, i.e. the cross-correlation between the observed and initial density fields, as well as on the BAO power spectrum. We study the influence of the spec-z errors on the fitted anisotropic BAO parameters $α_{\perp}$ and $α_{\parallel}$. The resulting systematic bias on $α_{\perp}$ and $α_{\parallel}$ is mild, mostly within $0.1$ per cent and $0.2$ per cent, respectively. Even with the spec-z errors, BAO reconstruction can still significantly reduce the systematic bias and statistical errors on the $α$ parameters. Furthermore, we vary the redshift uncertainty and study the reconstruction performance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the impact of spectroscopic redshift uncertainties and [O III]-Hβ interloper contamination on baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements in CSST-like slitless spectroscopic galaxy surveys. Using FastPM N-body simulations, the authors model how these errors damp the BAO signal and induce oscillations in the power spectrum broadband, then assess their effect on anisotropic BAO parameters before and after density field reconstruction, finding systematic biases well below 0.2% and demonstrating that reconstruction remains effective at mitigating both bias and statistical errors.
AI.motivation: With upcoming space-based telescopes like CSST performing slitless spectroscopic galaxy surveys, measured redshifts will suffer from uncertainties and interloper contamination due to low spectral resolution. Understanding and quantifying how these observational effects degrade BAO measurements—a key dark energy probe—is essential for accurate cosmological parameter constraints from future surveys.
AI.method: The study generates CSST-like slitless spectroscopic redshift samples using FastPM, an approximate N-body simulation code. Gaussian-distributed redshift uncertainties and [O III]-Hβ interlopers are injected into the samples. The interloper effect is modeled on the propagator (cross-correlation between observed and initial density fields) and on the BAO power spectrum. Anisotropic BAO parameters α⊥ and α∥ are fitted, and the impact of these errors is assessed both before and after density field reconstruction, including variations in the redshift uncertainty magnitude.
AI.result: Both redshift uncertainty and interlopers damp the BAO signal, with interlopers additionally inducing oscillations in the power spectrum broadband shape. The systematic biases on α⊥ and α∥ remain mild, mostly within 0.1% and 0.2% respectively. BAO reconstruction significantly reduces both systematic bias and statistical errors on the α parameters even in the presence of spec-z errors.
AI.conclusion: The spec-z errors from CSST-like slitless surveys, including redshift uncertainty and interloper contamination, introduce only modest systematic biases in BAO parameter estimation. Density field reconstruction remains effective in mitigating these effects, supporting the viability of BAO measurements as a dark energy probe in future slitless spectroscopic surveys.

title: Decoupling candidate dual AGN from chance superpositions in the GOTHIC survey via a deep-learning framework
comment: Submitted to MNRAS. Supplementary Material merged in the main text
summary: Dual active galactic nuclei (DAGN) mark a critical phase in the evolution of merging galaxies and the pairing of supermassive black holes, yet they remain difficult to identify in large imaging surveys because of projection effects and limited spatial resolution. Compact foreground stars and unresolved substructure can mimic dual nuclei through chance superposition, complicating automated detection. We revisit the 46,061 galaxies flagged but rejected as DAGN candidates by the GOTHIC pipeline, primarily because the two nuclei fell within the SDSS fibre aperture or exceeded its separation threshold. We train a supervised deep-learning framework based on the YOLOv11 oriented-bounding-box architecture on annotated SDSS imaging to separate genuine dual nuclei from foreground stellar contaminants and other spurious alignments. The final model attains a validation precision of 0.919, recall of 0.905, and $F_1$ of 0.912 for the dual-nuclei class, and yields 29,605 dual-nucleus candidates after removing star-dominated and blended detections. Structured visual inspection indicates that $54.5$--$62\%$ are consistent with genuine dual nuclei, implying $\sim(1.4$--$1.8)\times10^{4}$ plausible systems. Cross-calibrating the YOLO separation against the deterministic GOTHIC centroid measurement and restricting to the compact regime ($d \le 6.87''$) gives a conservative subset of $\sim 13{,}672$ candidates, reaching calibrated separations of $\sim 0.56''$. Spectroscopy of the most compact ($\le 1$~kpc) systems shows they are dominated by passive, absorption-line galaxies with no resolved double-peaked emission, so confirmation requires higher-resolution follow-up. The catalogue is a statistically refined list of candidates, not confirmed DAGN. Nonetheless, deep-learning detection substantially reduces contamination and expands the plausible DAGN census.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines 46,061 galaxies previously rejected as DAGN candidates by the GOTHIC pipeline, using a YOLOv11 oriented-bounding-box deep-learning model trained on SDSS imaging to separate genuine dual active galactic nuclei from foreground stars and spurious alignments. The model achieves 0.919 precision, 0.905 recall, and 0.912 F1, yielding 29,605 dual-nucleus candidates of which 54.5-62% pass visual inspection as plausible DAGN, with a conservative compact subset of ~13,672 candidates reaching calibrated separations of ~0.56 arcsec.
AI.motivation: Dual active galactic nuclei are important tracers of galaxy mergers and supermassive black hole pairing, but they are difficult to identify in large imaging surveys due to projection effects, limited resolution, and contamination from foreground stars and unresolved substructure that mimic dual nuclei.
AI.method: The authors retrain the GOTHIC-rejected sample (46,061 galaxies) through a supervised deep-learning framework based on the YOLOv11 oriented-bounding-box architecture, using annotated SDSS imaging. They cross-calibrate YOLO detections against the deterministic GOTHIC centroid measurements, apply a compact-regime cutoff (d ≤ 6.87''), and perform structured visual inspection and spectroscopic follow-up of the most compact systems.
AI.result: The model achieves validation precision of 0.919, recall of 0.905, and F1 of 0.912 for dual-nuclei detection. It yields 29,605 dual-nucleus candidates after removing star-dominated and blended detections, with 54.5-62% consistent with genuine dual nuclei (~1.4-1.8 × 10^4 plausible systems). A conservative subset of ~13,672 candidates reaches calibrated separations of ~0.56''. Spectroscopy of the most compact (≤1 kpc) systems shows passive, absorption-line galaxies without resolved double-peaked emission.
AI.conclusion: Deep-learning-based detection substantially reduces contamination in DAGN candidate identification and expands the plausible DAGN census, though the resulting catalogue represents statistically refined candidates rather than confirmed systems; compact candidates require higher-resolution follow-up for confirmation.

title: A "MeerKAT-meets-LOFAR" Study of 2A 0335+096: Discovery of a Complex 500 kpc Radio Halo in a Disturbed Cool-Core Cluster
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. Main article is 13 pages, appendix 3 pages
summary: The emerging picture of radio haloes and mini-haloes in galaxy clusters is more blurred and far less distinct than once thought. While both trace cosmic ray electrons and magnetic fields in the intracluster medium (ICM), our knowledge of the mechanisms powering these sources, their properties and their connection to cluster dynamics, is incomplete. We present new deep MeerKAT L-band (856$-$1712\,MHz) observations of the sloshing cool-core cluster 2A~0335+096, performed as part of the ``MeerKAT-meets-LOFAR'' mini-halo census, as well as reprocessed LOFAR 120$-$168\,MHz LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey data. We present highly sensitive radio continuum images, from which we perform a spectral analysis and a comparison of the thermal and non-thermal properties using reprocessed archival \textit{XMM-Newton} data. Our MeerKAT data reveal that the known mini-halo is embedded in a large-scale radio halo spanning up to 510\,kpc in this sloshing cluster, although only the inner mini-halo is detected by LOFAR. We find a typical steep spectrum of $α= -1.20 \pm 0.09$ for the mini-halo; the non-detection of the larger-scale halo by LOFAR indicates a spectral index no steeper than $-1.2$. Our results are broadly consistent with an interpretation of turbulent (re-)acceleration powered by sloshing within the cluster potential well. This work emphasises the need for using deep, high-dynamic multi-frequency radio observations in conjunction with high-quality X-ray observations to complete our understanding of the connection between radio halo properties and cluster dynamics.

AI.tldr: New deep MeerKAT and reprocessed LOFAR observations of the sloshing cool-core cluster 2A 0335+096 reveal that the known mini-halo is embedded within a large-scale radio halo spanning up to 510 kpc, with a steep mini-halo spectrum of α = -1.20 ± 0.09. The results support turbulent (re-)acceleration powered by sloshing and highlight the need for deep multi-frequency radio and X-ray observations to understand halo-cluster dynamics connections.
AI.motivation: To improve our incomplete understanding of radio haloes and mini-haloes in galaxy clusters—specifically their powering mechanisms, properties, and connection to cluster dynamics—by obtaining sensitive observations of a sloshing cool-core cluster where these source classes may coexist.
AI.method: Deep MeerKAT L-band (856-1712 MHz) observations and reprocessed LOFAR 120-168 MHz LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey data of 2A 0335+096, combined with reprocessed archival XMM-Newton X-ray data for thermal/non-thermal comparison. High-sensitivity radio continuum imaging enabled spectral index analysis and multi-wavelength comparisons.
AI.result: The mini-halo is embedded in a large-scale radio halo extending to 510 kpc, detected only by MeerKAT (not LOFAR). The mini-halo has a steep spectrum α = -1.20 ± 0.09. The LOFAR non-detection of the outer halo implies a spectral index no steeper than -1.2, and results are broadly consistent with turbulent (re-)acceleration from sloshing in the cluster potential well.
AI.conclusion: Deep, high-dynamic multi-frequency radio observations combined with high-quality X-ray data are essential to fully understand the connection between radio halo properties and cluster dynamics, with findings supporting sloshing-powered turbulent (re-)acceleration in this system.

title: SDSS-IV MaNGA: Star Formation Cessation in Low-redshift Galaxies. III. Dependence on Quenching Criteria
summary: This paper is the third in a series of studies investigating star formation cessation in nearby galaxies on kiloparsec scales. Using the final SDSS-IV MaNGA data release, we ask how the inferred importance of global, local, and environmental properties depends on the operational definition of quenched regions. We classify spaxels as star-forming, reliably quenched, or potentially quenched by accounting for measurement uncertainties, and train random forest classifiers with a parameter set chosen for direct comparison with previous work. For reliably quenched regions, the local stellar mass surface density $Σ_\ast$ consistently has the highest feature importance, independent of quenching definition. By contrast, the high importance of central velocity dispersion $σ_c$, previously interpreted as evidence for galaxy-wide AGN feedback, is recovered mainly when potentially quenched regions are included. The leading parameter also varies with stellar mass: $Σ_{\rm 1kpc}$ is most important below $\sim10^{10.2}\,\textrm{M}_{\odot}$, whereas local quantities such as $Σ_\ast$ and $σ_\ast$ become more prominent at high masses. These results show that quenching criteria and uncertainty treatment can reconcile apparently discrepant feature-importance studies. AGN-related processes may contribute to ambiguous regions, but the reliably quenched population is most tightly linked to high local stellar density.

AI.tldr: This study uses final SDSS-IV MaNGA data to examine how the importance of global, local, and environmental properties for predicting star formation cessation depends on the operational definition of quenched regions. Random forest classifiers show that local stellar mass surface density (Σ*) is most important for reliably quenched spaxels regardless of definition, while central velocity dispersion (σc)—previously linked to AGN feedback—only gains importance when potentially quenched regions are included. Feature importance also varies with stellar mass.
AI.motivation: Previous studies on what drives star formation cessation in galaxies have yielded apparently discrepant feature-importance results. This paper aims to reconcile these discrepancies by investigating whether differences in how quenched regions are operationally defined (accounting for measurement uncertainties) affect the inferred importance of global, local, and environmental properties.
AI.method: Using final SDSS-IV MaNGA data, spaxels are classified as star-forming, reliably quenched, or potentially quenched while accounting for measurement uncertainties. Random forest classifiers are trained with a parameter set chosen for direct comparison with previous work to assess feature importance under different quenching definitions and across stellar mass regimes.
AI.result: For reliably quenched regions, local stellar mass surface density (Σ*) consistently has the highest feature importance regardless of quenching definition. Central velocity dispersion (σc) is important mainly when potentially quenched regions are included. The leading parameter varies with stellar mass: Σ_1kpc dominates below ~10^10.2 M_sun, while local quantities Σ* and σ* become more prominent at high masses.
AI.conclusion: Quenching criteria and uncertainty treatment can reconcile apparently discrepant feature-importance studies. Reliably quenched populations are most tightly linked to high local stellar density, while AGN-related processes (indicated by σc) may contribute mainly to ambiguous or potentially quenched regions.

title: The Primordial power spectrum from the largest to smallest CMB scales
summary: We reconstruct the primordial power spectrum (PPS) across the full range of cosmological scales accessible to Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations. Using the Modified Richardson--Lucy algorithm, we perform free-form reconstructions through deconvolution of Planck PR3 and PR4, Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) DR6, and South Pole Telescope 3G (SPT-3G) D1 data. Across different regularization schemes, we find no evidence for significant deviations from a power-law primordial spectrum. The reconstructed spectra show a strong correlation between Planck and ACT, even at the level of localized features over their overlapping range, $0.07 < k < 0.14\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, demonstrating consistency between the two observations. Using a complementary parametric Bayesian reconstruction, we find that the previously discussed preference for a blueward tilt in the ACT data at small scales is preferred only at the $1σ$ level.

AI.tldr: This paper reconstructs the primordial power spectrum (PPS) across all CMB-observable cosmological scales using the Modified Richardson–Lucy deconvolution algorithm on Planck PR3/PR4, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data. No significant deviations from a power-law spectrum are found across different regularization schemes, and Planck and ACT reconstructions show strong correlation including localized features in the overlapping range. A complementary parametric Bayesian analysis finds the previously reported blueward tilt in ACT data at small scales is only preferred at ~1σ, suggesting it is not statistically significant.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the primordial power spectrum deviates from the standard power-law assumption, and to assess consistency between independent CMB experiments (Planck, ACT, SPT-3G) while evaluating the significance of previously reported spectral features such as a blueward tilt in ACT data.
AI.method: The authors use the Modified Richardson–Lucy algorithm to perform free-form (non-parametric) PPS reconstructions via deconvolution of multiple CMB datasets (Planck PR3 and PR4, ACT DR6, SPT-3G D1), employing various regularization schemes. They complement this with a parametric Bayesian reconstruction approach to test the significance of specific spectral features.
AI.result: No significant deviations from a scale-invariant power-law PPS are found across regularization schemes. Planck and ACT reconstructions show strong correlation, including localized features in the overlapping k-range (0.07–0.14 Mpc⁻¹). The previously favored blueward tilt in ACT small-scale data is preferred only at the 1σ level.
AI.conclusion: The primordial power spectrum is consistent with a power-law across all CMB-observable scales, and the apparent ACT blueward tilt at small scales is not statistically significant. The close agreement between independent experiments strengthens confidence in the standard cosmological model.

title: An HI study of a large sample of ultra-diffuse galaxies
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal; 25 pages, 10 figures
summary: By cross-matching the SMUDGes catalog with the FASHI and ALFALFA HI surveys, we construct an HI-detected sample of 112 ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) and 48 low-surface-brightness (LSB) galaxies, providing HI-based redshifts for 76 galaxies for the first time. Using DESI DR1 redshifts, we assemble an HI-non-detected sample of 168 galaxies for stacking analysis, with detections in two stellar mass bins below 10^{8.5} M_sun. Combining optical, UV, and HI data, we investigate stellar masses, star formation rates, gas fractions, and kinematics. We present a systematic analysis of the HI mass--optical size relation for UDGs and LSBs, showing both populations follow a mass--optical size scaling similar to normal galaxies, suggesting an average HI surface density, under the assumption that the optical size traces the extent of the HI distribution. Their stellar mass--size relation indicates nearly constant stellar surface densities for galaxies with central surface brightness mu_{0,g}>~24mag arcsec^{-2}, independent of UDG or LSB classification. Many UDGs and LSB galaxies are systematically offset from the baryonic Tully--Fisher relation toward higher baryonic masses at a given velocity, consistent with trends found in UDGs with resolved HI kinematics. Both populations exhibit low star formation efficiencies and long gas depletion times, supporting multiple formation pathways for UDGs.

AI.tldr: This paper cross-matches the SMUDGes catalog with FASHI and ALFALFA HI surveys to construct samples of HI-detected ultra-diffuse galaxies (112 UDGs) and low-surface-brightness galaxies (48 LSBs), providing new HI-based redshifts for 76 galaxies. Combining optical, UV, and HI data with DESI DR1 stacking analysis, the authors systematically investigate stellar masses, star formation rates, gas fractions, kinematics, and scaling relations, finding that UDGs and LSBs follow normal mass-size relations, are offset from the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation, and exhibit low star formation efficiencies with long gas depletion times, supporting multiple formation pathways.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the gas content, kinematics, and scaling relations of ultra-diffuse galaxies and low-surface-brightness galaxies using a large sample of HI-detected objects, addressing open questions about their formation mechanisms and whether they differ fundamentally from normal galaxies.
AI.method: Cross-matching the SMUDGes catalog with FASHI and ALFALFA HI surveys for HI-detected samples (112 UDGs, 48 LSBs), using DESI DR1 redshifts to build a stacking sample of 168 HI-non-detected galaxies. Analysis combines optical, UV, and HI data to derive stellar masses, star formation rates, gas fractions, and kinematics, with stacking detections in two stellar mass bins below 10^8.5 M_sun.
AI.result: Both UDGs and LSBs follow the HI mass-optical size relation of normal galaxies. The stellar mass-size relation shows nearly constant stellar surface densities for galaxies with central surface brightness mu_{0,g} > ~24 mag arcsec^-2, independent of classification. Many UDGs and LSBs are systematically offset from the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation toward higher baryonic masses at fixed velocity. Both populations show low star formation efficiencies and long gas depletion times, with stacking detections achieved in two low stellar mass bins.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that UDGs and LSBs are not fundamentally different from normal galaxies in their scaling relations, but their deviations from the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation and low star formation efficiencies support multiple formation pathways for ultra-diffuse galaxies.

title: Dark-to-black super-accretion as a spin-imprinting mechanism for supermassive Kerr black holes
summary: The existence of supermassive black holes with masses $M\gtrsim10^9\,M_{\odot}$ and large dimensionless spins $χ\sim0.9-0.99$ at high redshift remains a challenge to our understanding of the early Universe. In this work, we study the adiabatic co-evolution of a Kerr black hole seed surrounded by two ultralight scalar dark matter clouds occupying different bound states, and show that this configuration allows the black hole to grow into the supermassive mass range while imprinting a characteristic final spin. The evolution proceeds through two stages. During the first stage, a spherical cloud described by the $\ell=0$ mode is completely depleted through a runaway dark-to-black accretion mechanism on a timescale of hundreds of millions of years for boson masses $μ\sim10^{-18}-10^{-17}\,\mathrm{eV}$. Since the accreted material does not carry angular momentum, the black hole spin is universally driven to $χ\simeq0$, independently of its initial spin. Throughout this stage, the second cloud, described by the $\ell=m=1$ mode, remains in the superradiant regime with negligible evolution. However, once the first stage is completed, this cloud transitions to the accreting regime, rapidly transferring both mass and angular momentum to the black hole. Starting from $χ\simeq0$, the black hole spin increases until the evolution self-consistently saturates close to the threshold $χ_{\rm sat}$, defined by the condition $Ω_H(χ_{\rm sat})=μ$, on an e-folding timescale of thousands of years, orders of magnitude shorter than the first stage. This final saturation spin is largely independent of both the initial black hole spin and the mass of the secondary cloud, providing a spin-imprinting mechanism in which the primordial spin is first erased by spherical accretion and then reset to a value determined only by the boson mass and the final black hole mass.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the adiabatic co-evolution of a Kerr black hole seed with two ultralight scalar dark matter clouds in different bound states, showing that this configuration enables supermassive black hole growth while imprinting a characteristic final spin through a two-stage process.
AI.motivation: The existence of supermassive black holes with masses >10^9 solar masses and large spins at high redshift challenges our understanding of the early Universe. The authors aim to explain this growth while also understanding spin evolution.
AI.method: The authors study the adiabatic co-evolution of a Kerr black hole seed with two ultralight scalar dark matter clouds occupying different bound states (ℓ=0 spherical mode and ℓ=m=1 mode). The evolution proceeds in two stages: first, the spherical cloud is depleted via runaway dark-to-black accretion; second, the ℓ=m=1 cloud transitions to the accreting regime, transferring mass and angular momentum to the black hole.
AI.result: During the first stage (hundreds of millions of years timescale for boson masses μ~10^-18-10^-17 eV), spherical accretion drives the black hole spin universally to χ≃0 regardless of initial spin. In the second stage (e-folding timescale of thousands of years), the spin increases and self-consistently saturates near the threshold χ_sat defined by Ω_H(χ_sat)=μ. The final saturation spin depends mainly on boson mass and final black hole mass, independent of initial spin and secondary cloud mass.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a spin-imprinting mechanism in which the primordial black hole spin is first erased by spherical accretion and then reset to a value determined only by the boson mass and the final black hole mass, offering a novel pathway for supermassive black hole formation with predictable final spin.

title: Synchrotron filaments in radio galaxies: rarity, stability, and environmental influences from LOFAR and ROSAT observations
summary: We present a systematic investigation of filamentary synchrotron structures in radio galaxies, using deep 144 MHz observations from the LOFAR Two-Metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) in combination with archival ROSAT X-ray data. These narrow, collimated features, linking radio lobes and often aligned with jet axes, are rare: our visual inspection of 548 cluster-associated sources identified 12 candidates (~2.2%), of which three exhibit clearly resolved filaments suitable for detailed X-ray and synchrotron minimum pressure analysis. Minimum pressures in these filaments are consistently lower than the ambient thermal pressure derived from X-ray measurements. This disparity implies a role for external confinement in filament stability, aligning with theoretical predictions of thermal pressure support and potentially toroidal magnetic field configurations. We discuss filament formation scenarios, including relic AGN outflows, magnetic draping, and plasma instabilities. Our findings highlight the utility of filamentary structures as probes of intracluster magnetic field topology and AGN feedback, and demonstrate the need for high-resolution, multi-frequency studies to constrain their origin and evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates rare filamentary synchrotron structures in radio galaxies using LOFAR LoTSS 144 MHz and archival ROSAT X-ray data. Among 548 cluster-associated sources, 12 candidates (~2.2%) were found, with three clearly resolved filaments analyzed in detail. Filament minimum pressures are consistently lower than ambient thermal pressure, implying external confinement and supporting thermal pressure support with potentially toroidal magnetic field configurations. The authors discuss formation scenarios (relic AGN outflows, magnetic draping, plasma instabilities) and advocate for high-resolution multi-frequency follow-up.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand the nature, prevalence, and physical conditions of rare filamentary synchrotron structures in radio galaxies, and to assess how they probe intracluster magnetic field topology and AGN feedback mechanisms.
AI.method: Visual inspection of 548 cluster-associated sources from LoTSS 144 MHz observations, combined with archival ROSAT X-ray data for pressure analysis; detailed X-ray and synchrotron minimum pressure comparisons were performed on three clearly resolved filament candidates.
AI.result: 12 filament candidates identified (~2.2% occurrence). Filament minimum pressures are consistently below ambient X-ray-derived thermal pressures, indicating external confinement. Three filaments were suitable for detailed X-ray and pressure analysis.
AI.conclusion: Filamentary structures are rare but useful probes of intracluster magnetic field topology and AGN feedback. Their pressure imbalance suggests external thermal confinement and potentially toroidal magnetic field configurations. High-resolution, multi-frequency observations are needed to constrain filament origin and evolution.

title: Gaussian process reconstruction of scalar field dynamics from recent cosmological data
summary: We reconstruct the late-time expansion history and dark energy dynamics using available cosmological data. We consider dark energy as an effective minimally coupled canonical scalar field without assuming a specific form for its potential. For reconstruction, we use Gaussian Process (GP) regression with a joint dataset consisting of 32 cosmic chronometer measurements (CC32), DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation data, three Type Ia supernova compilations (Pantheon+, Union3, and DES Y5), and compressed CMB distance priors. From the reconstructed Hubble parameter and its derivatives, we obtain the scalar field kinetic and potential energy densities, the equation of state $w(z)$, and the dimensionless slope parameter $|λ(z)|$ of the scalar field potential.
